Disease Outbreak Disrupts Ghana’s Electric Utilities Workforce

A disease outbreak is sweeping through the workforce of Ghana’s electric utilities industry, disrupting operations and threatening the stability of electricity supply in several regions, according to company officials and union representatives.

Electricity Co Of Ghana Ltd, the nation’s largest power distribution company, confirmed on Thursday that a significant number of its employees at multiple sites have reported symptoms associated with the outbreak, identified by health authorities as a severe strain of influenza. The company has reduced its field operations in the Eastern, Ashanti, and Greater Accra regions, citing staff shortages and the need to prevent further spread among workers.

Kwame Adjei, spokesperson for Electricity Co Of Ghana Ltd, said, “About 18% of our technical staff are currently off duty due to illness, which has forced us to delay scheduled maintenance and some repair works. Our priority is the health of our employees and the safety of the communities we serve.”

The outbreak, which first emerged at a substation in Koforidua last week, has now affected at least two other firms in the sector, including the privately owned Voltic Power Services. The Ghana Energy Workers Union estimates that as many as 400 employees across the industry are currently unwell or quarantined.

Residents have reported extended power outages in parts of Kumasi and Tema, with response teams stretched thin. “Normally they would fix faults within hours, but now, it’s taking more than a day,” said Ama Owusu, a local resident in Kumasi.

Industry analyst Daniel Mensah noted, “With so many key personnel absent, routine maintenance, emergency repairs, and system upgrades are being postponed. The risk of network failures increases the longer this persists.”

The Ghana Utilities Regulatory Commission has asked companies to provide daily updates on staffing and service levels. “We are monitoring the situation closely and urge all companies to prioritize health protocols,” said a Commission statement.

As the outbreak continues, there is growing concern about the ability of the industry to maintain stable electricity delivery until workforces recover.
